title: The Lesson I Learned From Enoch’s Disappearance
paragraphs: The Lesson I Learned From Enoch’s Disappearance
There are stories in Scripture that comfort us.
There are stories that challenge us.
And then there are stories that haunt us.
For me, the story of Enoch has always been one of those stories.
He appears briefly. Says almost nothing. Leaves almost no details behind.
Just a man who walked with God.
Sometimes I wonder if that is precisely why God preserved his story.
Because in a world obsessed with being noticed, Enoch teaches us what it means to be known by God.
The entire account in Genesis is only a few verses long.

“Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.”
(Genesis 5:24)
In Hebrew, the phrase is astonishingly simple:
The verb used here is not merely walking from one place to another.
It carries the sense of continual movement, habitual fellowship, an ongoing lifestyle.
This was not a man who occasionally visited God.
This was a man who lived in God’s presence.
And perhaps that is what unsettles me.
Because when I read about Enoch, I immediately realize how much of my own life can become distracted.
Filled with notifications, deadlines, worries, ambitions, fears, and endless noise.
Meanwhile, Enoch’s entire legacy can be summarized in four words:
We live in a generation where everyone wants influence.
Yet Enoch reminds us that heaven measures greatness differently.
The deeper I study Enoch, the more remarkable his life becomes.
He did not live in a godly generation.
In fact, he lived in one of the darkest periods in human history.
The corruption that would eventually lead to Noah’s flood was already growing.
Humanity was drifting further from God.
The New Testament reveals even more.
“By faith Enoch was taken away so that he did not see death.”
The word metetethē means moved from one place to another.
Death never became the final chapter of his earthly story.
One day walking with God on earth.
The next walking with God in eternity.
The lesson that shattered me is this:
It was the result of thousands of ordinary days.
We often focus on the moment God took him.
God focuses on the years before.
But you cannot separate the two.
The destination was shaped by the direction.
The ending was shaped by the walk.
And maybe that is exactly what some of us need to hear.
Because we keep waiting for God to do something extraordinary while ignoring the ordinary places where He is already calling us to follow Him.
The parent raising children in faith.
The worker choosing integrity when nobody is watching.
The believer fighting temptation in secret.
The husband learning to love sacrificially.
The young adult pursuing holiness in a culture that mocks purity.
The older saint praying faithfully for family members who still do not know Christ.
Enoch teaches us that God is deeply interested in what happens when nobody else is watching.
There is another detail that often gets overlooked.
The name “Enoch” in Hebrew is חֲנוֹךְ (Chanokh), carrying the idea of dedication or consecration.
A life belonging to someone else.
That resonates deeply because the Gospel itself calls believers into that same reality.
We were bought with a price.
The ultimate lesson of Enoch is not actually about Enoch.
Every faithful biblical story eventually points beyond itself.
Jesus is God who walked among us.
Jesus perfectly pleased the Father in everything.
Jesus ascended into heaven after conquering sin, death, and the grave forever.
The story reaches its fulfillment in Christ.
That is why the Gospel changes everything.
Because none of us have walked with God perfectly.
Some have carried shame for years.
Some have scars nobody knows about.
Some have built entire identities around mistakes they cannot seem to escape.
Yet the message of Jesus is not that we must earn our way back.
The message of Jesus is that He came to bring us back.
This is where our story always returns.
Scripture is filled with people whose failures should have been their final chapter.
Yet Jesus continually transforms disgrace into redemption.
That is what makes the Gospel unlike any other message in human history.
God does not merely improve people.
Perhaps the reason Enoch’s story feels so powerful is because every believer is ultimately moving toward the same destination.
The goal of Christianity has never been simply avoiding hell.
The goal has always been God Himself.
And every day we choose to walk with Christ, we take another step toward home.
Maybe that is the question Enoch leaves behind for every generation:
What direction are your feet moving?
Because eventually everyone arrives where they have been walking.
I stopped asking whether I was accomplishing enough.
I started asking whether I was walking closely enough.
I stopped obsessing over being known.
I stopped measuring success by visibility.
I started measuring it by faithfulness.
If this message stirred something in your spirit, do not keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
Because every share helps spread the Gospel.
Every testimony reminds someone they are not alone.
And every soul reached is worth it.
One day, the achievements people celebrated about you will be forgotten.
But the steps you took with Jesus will echo forever.
